newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S. and Poland to build Holocaust memorial.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. and Poland to build Holocaust memorial.

text.p: Poland and the United States are cooperating in an unprecedented joint project to build a major Holocaust memorial on the site of a Nazi extermination camp in Poland.

The monument will be built at Belzec, south of the city of Lublin in eastern Poland, where Nazis murdered an estimated 600,000 Jews. Belzec was the first place the Germans erected permanent gas chambers and marked a decisive phase in the Final Solution, the Nazi plan to kill all the Jews of Europe.

There is a small memorial on the site, erected in the 1960s by the former Communist authorities in Poland, which depicts two emaciated figures clutching each other. But it is falling apart with neglect and the site is overgrown with weeds and strewn with garbage.

"Not only is the monument decaying, it has no symbolic significance. It does not even mention the fact that virtually all the victims of Belzec were Jews," said Jacek Nowokowski, director of collections and acquisitions at the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, who is managing the U.S. side of the project.

After some family members of victims of Belzec complained about the neglect they found at the site, officials from the museum, an arm of the U.S. federal government, approached the Polish authorities to build a new memorial.

"Belzec has been terribly neglected despite the fact that it was one of the major Nazi killing centres," said museum chairman Miles Lerman, whose parents were murdered there. "It is essential that we restore it as a major centre of remembrance."

Lerman signed an agreement last year with Andrzej Przewoznik, director of the Council for the Protection of the Memory of Combat and Martyrdom in Poland, the state body responsible for preserving the hundreds of Second World War martrydom sites in the country. Under the agreement, seven eminent Polish architects, each of whom has already designed at least one Holocaust memorial, were invited to take part in a competition for the new design. A panel of Polish and American experts will choose the winning entry this year.

"This year, in April, we will be able to view the new design for a memorial at the site of the former extermination camp of Belzec," Przewoznik said in a statement issued in Warsaw. "In its central point, there will be a new monument erected in the place of the old, already in a very bad technical condition. The new monument will symbolise the tragic history of Belzec."
The joint project is emerging as an opportunity to repair ties between Jews and Poles, severely strained after a series of squabbles regarding the Auschwitz-Birkenau death camp.

Jewish leaders, noting that 90 percent of the victims at Auschwitz were Jewish, were angry that official ceremonies of the 50th anniversary of its liberation in 1995 did not include Jewish prayers for the dead. They also clashed bitterly over a Catholic Carmelite Convent at Auschwitz, since removed, which Jews believed had no place there.
Belzec was one of six extermination camps erected by the Nazis. The other five were Treblinka, Sobibor, Majdanek, Auschwitz-Birkenau and Chelmno.

The camp began operating in March 1942. Victims were packed tightly into four gas chambers and killed by carbon monoxide generated from a huge aircraft engine, with some taking as long as 35 minutes to die. Their naked bodies were dumped in trenches. There were only two recorded survivors, neither of whom is still alive.

The Nazis had built Belzec to destroy the centuries-old Jewish communities of southern and eastern Poland. In 1942, that job done, they closed the camp. They later tried to hide their crime, burning the bodies and grinding up the bones. But visitors to Belzec still find human bone fragments littering the ground.
